Scott's restored versions stripped away much of that interference, allowing the questions surrounding Deckard, Rachael, and what separates humans from replicants to remain unresolved. Its visual DNA became almost unavoidable in future science fiction, while Blade Runner 2049 later expanded the different types of replicants and philosophical questions of the original. Hugh Jackman's characters exist across different periods that may be literal, symbolic, or both, while Aronofsky uses recurring images rather than straightforward explanations to connect them. That ambiguity frustrated plenty of critics in 2006. It is also why the movie rewards revisiting. The Fountain never became universally loved, but its cult reputation makes the original hostility look increasingly shortsighted.

A.I. Artificial Intelligence seemed almost designed to confuse expectations in 2001. Stanley Kubrick had developed the project for years before Steven Spielberg finally directed it, leaving critics eager to identify where one filmmaker supposedly ended and the other began. The final act became especially contentious, with Spielberg accused of softening Kubrick's darker vision.

That interpretation aged awkwardly once more became known about the production. Many elements dismissed as sentimental Spielberg touches, including much of the ending, originated with Kubrick's conception of the story. Roger Ebert also famously reconsidered the film, eventually adding it to his Great Movies collection after criticizing aspects of it on release. Seen now, David's endless desire to be loved feels far crueler than the supposedly comforting ending suggests. Humanity disappears; the machine programmed to love is still waiting for someone to love him back.
